source_document.body:
EICMA 2026 • Honda Has a Taste of the e-MTB World with the RN0 Motor-Assisted Bicycle
Moparhead Went To Buy a '57 Chrysler New Yorker, Drove Home in a Super-Rare 1963 Chrysler 300J
56 photos
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile
Back in the early sixties, Ma’ Mopar had a problem: the cars weren’t the best-looking ones in Motor City, but its engines were gunning for apex predator crowns all over the place. That conundrum put buyers under a lot of second-though indecision, and nothing illustrates that hesitation more than the elusive Chrysler 300J from 1963. Sources note that around 100 are known today, which is an overwhelming 25% of all original production. One of those incredible relics just made a guest star appearance at MCACN 2026.
Nothing tests a car guy’s poker face quite like showing up to buy one classic Mopar and watching the seller suddenly develop cold feet. Back in 2025, Omaha enthusiast Kurt Brueske drove out to inspect an all-original, 40,000-mile 1957 Chrysler New Yorker coupe finished in Ruby Red with a black roof. His buddy chickened out at the eleventh hour, then casually offered his 1963 Chrysler 300J instead. Brueske barely blinked.
That glorious consolation prize recently stole the spotlight at the Muscle Car and Corvette Nationals, the grand assembly of classic Americana royalty in Rosemont, Illinois. That’s a stone’s throw away from Chicago, which is where Lou Costabile hangs around when he’s not shooting classics at point blank. With his camera!
The 300J is a car of many special traits, but the fender tag is not one of those. It doesn’t have one. Look all you like, take the sonar and the magnifying glass underhood and the greatest team of detectives, and you still won’t be able to locate a fender tag. Mostly because it’s not on the fenders, hence it can’t be a fender tag. But more importantly, because it’s not in the engine bay.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Chrysler tucked the 1963 trim tag down by the driver-side door hinge. It confirms body code 842 for the coupe, paint code WW1 for Oyster White, and rich Claret metallic-red leather. Wearing Nebraska plate 80-121, the hardtop fits Brueske’s Omaha club pedigree beside his 1962 300H. Even those rocket-nozzle taillights are pure "unobtainium," miraculous new-old-stock spares a previous owner somehow unearthed (probably from the end of the rainbow).
Climb inside and the 1963 cabin feels like a mid-century lounge with an attitude problem. You grip a squared steering wheel shaped like a vintage television screen (alright, anyone 40 and younger, go look it up), facing pushbutton TorqueFlite keys, a 150-mph speedometer, a console tachometer, and a low air-conditioning vent cryptically nicknamed a "crotch cooler," because of its direct line of sight to the target.
Locking the door requires pushing the interior handle forward – I so wish they made cool features like this standard again! – and don’t even bother to read the tach while driving at night. Why did carmakers choose to put the rev gauge on the center console, and make it about the size of a wristwatch is anyone’s guess.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile I’m putting my money on the fact that people were sharper in more ways than today, and could actually use a rotary-dial perpetual calendar without asking a computer for directions. All that executive eccentricity made total sense for Chrysler’s legendary Letter Series, born in 1955 when the C-300 welded NASCAR thunder onto country-club luxury.
Across eleven consecutive model years from 1955 through 1965, Chrysler marched alphabetically from C-300 to 300L, cranking out just 16,857 letter cars, a microscopic 1.29% of total brand output. In 1970, the 300 Hurst revival briefly crashed the party with 503 more brutes, sealing the bloodline’s cult aura. No, I don’t think the 300M from this millennium is a worthy heir to the Letter Series throne.
When the ninth installment arrived for 1963, Highland Park quietly skipped the letter "I" because Detroit figured shoppers might confuse it with the numeral 1. Thus, the 300J was born, wearing crisp, finless sheetmetal representing Virgil Exner’s final bow before former Ford stylist Elwood Engel took over in 1962. Study the scalloped C-pillar and recessed, Thunderbird-like taillights, though, and you can already spot Engel’s sharp fingerprints creeping into the metal.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Unfortunately for Chrysler’s bean counters, buyers stayed away in droves, turning the 1963 Chrysler 300J into the scarcest Letter Series car ever cobbled together. Between October 22, 1962, and June 18, 1963, assembly stalled at exactly 400 cars. Every single one of those 400 units rolled out as a two-door hardtop coupe. Drop-top fans defected to the cheaper, non-letter 300 Sport Series, which even paced the 1963 Indy 500.
Slice those 400 coupes by drivetrain and the rarity gets downright absurd. Exactly 393 buyers stuck with the standard pushbutton three-speed TorqueFlite automatic paired to a 3.23:1 rear axle, leaving a microscopic seven daredevils who checked the no-cost box for the heavy-duty, floor-shifted 3-speed manual and its 3.91:1 Sure-Grip differential.
Under the hood, nobody hesitated: all 400 units of the “Three Hundred J” (that’s what the emblems say) roared out of Detroit packing the exclusive 390-horsepower, 413-cubic-inch short-ram V8.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile One glance at the window sticker explains why showrooms stayed quiet. A brand-new 1963 300J demanded a stiff $5,200 base price, towering over the $3,400 base 300 Sport parked nearby. Because the 390-horsepower 413 Wedge came baked into the ticket, Chrysler listed no regular optional engine or upgrade price, though competition-spec 426-cubic-inch Maximum Performance Wedge monsters existed via unpriced special order for dedicated racers.
Still, anybody grumbling about the tab stopped complaining once that broad hood popped open. Chrysler’s cast-iron, overhead-valve 413-cubic-inch (6.8-liter) wedge V8 featured a 9.6:1 compression, solid lifters, a 268-degree camshaft, and high-flow cast-iron headers. Crowned by aluminum 15-inch cross-ram manifolds feeding twin Carter AFB four-barrel carburetors, it churned out 390 horsepower at 4,800 rpm and a rib-cracking 485 lb-ft of torque at 3,600 rpm (395 PS, 658 Nm).
Dyno engineers had learned a clever trick since the 30-inch long-ram intakes of 1960 and 1961: opening internal plenum passages to 15 inches shifted that ram-charging torque wallop from roughly 2,200 rpm up near 3,000 rpm. As Brueske gleefully noted, this tailored heavyweight matched an A12 Road Runner’s factory 390-horsepower punch. Shoving 4,000 pounds along a 122-inch wheelbase, an automatic 300J blasted from 0 to 60 mph in 8.0 seconds flat.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Keep your right loafer buried and the big Chrysler stormed through the quarter-mile in 15.4 to 15.8 seconds at up to 96 mph before topping out at a hair-raising 142 mph. Naturally, accountants panicked after 1963. For the 1964 300K, Chrysler slashed the price, demoted the short-ram V8 to an option, ditched standard leather, and swapped the 150-mph speedometer for a tame 120-mph dial, boosting volume to 3,647 cars.
That sensible corporate retreat accidentally crowned the 1963 300J as the final, unfiltered "banker's hot rod," all silk suit on the outside and freight-train menace underneath. When Brueske finally pointed this amazing power cruiser toward Nebraska in 2025, he felt every ounce of that effortless cross-ram shove firsthand. Sure, he missed out on his buddy’s 1957 New Yorker, yet stumbling backward into a 1-of-400 Mopar icon might be the luckiest detour ever.
